title: Best Attic Dehumidifier (2026): Ductable, Heat-Rated Picks
h1: The Best Attic Dehumidifiers for Heat, Cold and Tight Spaces
dek: Attics are hot in July, freezing in January and miles from a drain. These are the dehumidifiers built to cope.
description: The best attic dehumidifier picks of 2026: ductable, wide-temperature commercial units for real attics, plus a pump-equipped portable for finished ones.
intro: An **attic dehumidifier** has a harder job than almost any other. The space bakes in summer, chills in winter, is awkward to reach and almost never has a floor drain or a handy outlet. A unit designed for a basement or bedroom can shut down on a sweltering afternoon or ice over during a cold snap.

Attics also collect moisture that other rooms don’t: bathroom and kitchen fans that dump humid air into the attic instead of outdoors, slow roof leaks, and meltwater from ice dams. Left alone, that moisture soaks insulation, stains ceilings and feeds mold long before anyone notices.
We focused on units with wide published operating ranges, duct connections that reach past trusses and knee walls, and drainage that doesn’t depend on you climbing a ladder to empty a bucket.
topPicksLead: For most attics, the **AlorAir Sentinel HDi90** is the one to get: it ducts dry air to hard-to-reach sections and is rated to run from 33.8°F to 104°F.

blocks.text: A typical room dehumidifier is designed for roughly 65–95°F. An unconditioned attic routinely leaves that range at both ends, which is why specs matter more here than anywhere else in the house.

We don’t lab-test. We compared manufacturer spec sheets for operating temperature range, AHAM and DOE capacity ratings, duct options and drainage, and checked manuals for clearance and installation requirements. We then read owner and installer reviews for problems specific to attic use, like units overheating, pumps failing and condensate lines freezing.
Published operating range came first, followed by ducting, drainage, capacity and serviceability — because a unit you can’t easily reach needs to run reliably without attention.

sections.heading: What to look for in an attic dehumidifier

items.label: A wide operating-temperature range
items.text: Read the datasheet, not the product photo. Commercial units rated to about 34–104°F handle attics; standard portables don’t.

items.label: Ducting for divided attics
items.text: Trusses and knee walls block airflow. A ductable unit reaches spaces a stationary one never dries.

items.label: A pump or long drain line
items.text: Attics rarely have a floor drain. An attic dehumidifier with a pump is close to mandatory unless a gravity line can run down to a drain.

items.label: Capacity for the whole space
items.text: About 55 pints (AHAM) for a small attic, 70–90 for a typical one, 150+ for large or multi-section attics.

items.label: Remote monitoring
items.text: A remote sensor or wired control saves trips up the ladder.

sections.heading: Should you put a dehumidifier in your attic?

blocks.text: Sometimes — but fix the source first. In a conventional vented attic, moisture problems usually come from bath or kitchen fans venting into the attic, air leaking up from the living space, roof leaks or blocked soffit vents. Sealing and venting those properly often solves the problem without a machine.
A dehumidifier earns its place when humidity stays high after those fixes, when you’re drying out after a leak, or when the attic is sealed and insulated with spray foam.

An attic sealed with spray foam on the roof deck is unvented — it sits inside the home’s conditioned envelope. Without air exchange, moisture from the house can build up there. Building codes call for some form of conditioning in unvented attics, and newer code editions recognize dehumidification as one option. A ducted whole-house unit or a ductable commercial model is usually the right tool.

For a long-term solution, a ducted whole-house dehumidifier can be installed in a conditioned attic and tied into the HVAC system with a hard-plumbed condensate line. See our [whole-house dehumidifier installation](/guides/whole-house-dehumidifier-installation/) guide for what that involves.

sections.heading: Will a dehumidifier stop ice dams?

blocks.text: Not on its own. Ice dams form when heat escaping into the attic melts snow on the roof, and the water refreezes at the colder eaves. The fix is insulation and air sealing on the attic floor plus good roof ventilation.

blocks.title: What the dehumidifier does do
blocks.text: It manages the moisture that ice dams and roof leaks push into the attic — condensation on the roof deck, damp insulation and the mold that follows. Most attics need both fixes working together.

The **AlorAir Sentinel HDi90** is the best attic dehumidifier for most homes, combining full-attic capacity, ducting and a wide operating range. Choose the **Waykar 158-Pint Dual Duct** for large, divided attics, the **AlorAir HD55** for a small or hard-to-reach space, and the **Honeywell TPFIT50PWK** only for a finished attic room. Whatever you buy, fix venting and insulation problems first — a dehumidifier manages attic moisture, but it can’t stop the source. If mold is already present, read [does a dehumidifier help with mold](/guides/does-a-dehumidifier-help-with-mold/) before you start.

faqs.q: What is the best attic dehumidifier?
faqs.a: The AlorAir Sentinel HDi90 for most attics. It’s rated at 90 pints a day (AHAM), connects to ductwork to reach far sections and has a published 33.8–104°F operating range.

faqs.q: Can you put a dehumidifier in the attic?
faqs.a: Yes, if it’s rated for attic conditions. Standard room units are built for about 65–95°F and can fail in an unfinished attic. Commercial models with wide operating ranges, ducting and pump or gravity drainage are designed for it.

faqs.q: Should I put a dehumidifier in my attic?
faqs.a: First fix the usual causes — exhaust fans venting into the attic, air leaks, roof leaks and blocked vents. Add a dehumidifier if humidity stays high afterward, after a leak, or in a sealed spray foam attic.

faqs.q: Do spray foam attics need a dehumidifier?
faqs.a: Often. Spray foam creates an unvented attic inside the conditioned envelope, where moisture can accumulate. Codes require some form of conditioning, and dehumidification is a common way to provide it.

faqs.q: What size dehumidifier do I need for an attic?
faqs.a: About 55 pints (AHAM) for an attic under 1,300 sq ft, 70–90 pints for a typical full attic and 150+ pints or a dual-duct design for large or multi-section attics over about 2,500 sq ft.

faqs.q: Do I need an attic dehumidifier with a pump?
faqs.a: Usually. Attics seldom have a floor drain, so you need either a built-in pump or a gravity line that can run downhill to a drain. Emptying a bucket in an attic isn’t realistic.

faqs.q: Will a dehumidifier prevent ice dams?
faqs.a: No. Ice dams are caused by heat loss into the attic. A dehumidifier controls the resulting moisture, but insulation, air sealing and ventilation are what stop ice dams.
